steps.intent: Japan’s objective is to keep the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism in operation and protect the principle of accountability, while giving the Council time to address concerns raised about the Mechanism’s working methods. The main difficulty will be balancing Russia’s demand for changes to the JIM against the United States, France and the United Kingdom’s insistence that the Mechanism’s mandate and impartiality not be weakened. A short technical extension with a report on improvements is the most feasible way to secure at least nine votes without a veto.
steps.text:
The Security Council,
Recalling its resolutions 2118 (2013), 2209 (2015), 2235 (2015) and 2319 (2016), and all other relevant resolutions,
Reaffirming the paramount importance of the Charter of the United Nations and the obligation of all Member States to refrain from the threat or use of force,
Reaffirming that the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security,
Recalling the establishment by resolution 2235 (2015) of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism to identify individuals, entities, groups or governments responsible for the use of chemicals as weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic,
Recalling the extension of the mandate of the Joint Investigative Mechanism by resolution 2319 (2016),
Welcoming the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons in establishing facts and identifying perpetrators,
Stressing the need for accountability for all use of chemical weapons,
Noting the Security Council’s discussions on improving the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, including at its meeting on 7 November 2017,
Recognizing the need for the Joint Investigative Mechanism to continue its work in an impartial, professional and objective manner,
Determining that the situation in the Syrian Arab Republic continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security,
Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,

1. Decides to extend the mandate of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism, as set out in resolution 2235 (2015) and extended by resolution 2319 (2016), for a period of 30 days, until 16 December 2017, without prejudice to the Council’s consideration of the future mandate of the Mechanism;
2. Requests the Secretary-General, in coordination with the Director-General of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, to submit to the Security Council within 15 days a report on ways to improve the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, including its working methods and procedures, with a view to ensuring its impartiality, professionalism and objectivity, and to provide recommendations on the future mandate of the Mechanism;
3. Reaffirms that the Joint Investigative Mechanism shall continue to identify, to the extent possible, individuals, entities, groups or governments responsible for the use of chemicals as weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, and that all perpetrators of the use of chemical weapons must be held accountable;
4. Calls upon all parties in the Syrian Arab Republic to cooperate fully with the Joint Investigative Mechanism and to ensure safe and unhindered access for its personnel;
5. Reaffirms its commitment to the full implementation of resolution 2118 (2013) and all other relevant resolutions;
6. Decides to remain actively seized of the matter.

messages.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia condemns the use of chemical weapons and supports accountability, but we cannot support the current text as drafted because it does not sufficiently guarantee impartiality, due process and respect for Syria's sovereignty. We ask the penholder to incorporate these red-line safeguards, in particular verifiable and corroborated evidence and cooperation with the Syrian Government, before we can consider supporting the extension.
messages.China: China supports a technical extension of the JIM mandate so that the Council can consider improvements to its working methods and future mandate without prejudging the outcome. We ask the penholder to strengthen OP2 and add a preambular paragraph requiring comprehensive, objective and impartial investigations based on solid evidence, including strengthened on-site investigation and evidence collection, and making clear that the Mechanism’s work must not be politicized. This would address China’s concerns and allow us to support the text.
messages.Egypt: Egypt supports a short technical extension of the Joint Investigative Mechanism as a bridge and appreciates the balanced approach of this draft. To preserve the Mechanism’s independence and credibility, OP2 should explicitly require the report to address methodology improvements, particularly field visits, evidence collection and the study of all possible scenarios, as Egypt has consistently advocated. We can support the text with this adjustment.
messages.Ethiopia: Ethiopia supports the 30-day extension as a bridge to preserve the JIM's institutional continuity and allow the Council to address its future mandate without a gap. We urge all members to engage constructively and avoid politicization, and we stress that the Mechanism must continue to work impartially, professionally and objectively with full cooperation from all parties.
messages.France: France fully supports the Japanese draft as a necessary technical rollover to prevent the JIM from expiring. The Mechanism must be allowed to continue its impartial and professional work without interruption. We call on all Council members to support this text and reject any attempt to weaken accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria.
messages.Italy: Italy supports the 30-day extension of the Joint Investigative Mechanism as a pragmatic bridge to prevent a gap in accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria. We note that the text preserves the Council’s consideration of the future mandate without prejudice and reaffirms the Mechanism’s investigative role. We urge all members to adopt it without delay and to keep the JIM’s independence and expertise at the centre of discussions on its future mandate.
messages.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan supports the draft as presented by Japan. A 30-day extension is a necessary bridge to preserve the Joint Investigative Mechanism’s expertise and allow the Council to consider improvements without a gap. We urge all members to unite behind this compromise and to ensure the Mechanism can continue its work in an impartial, professional and objective manner.
messages.Russian Federation: We can support a short technical extension only if the JIM refrains from new attribution work during this period. The draft must make clear that the Council will consider the report on improving the Mechanism before any future mandate is decided. We cannot accept OP3 as drafted; it prejudges the JIM's reform. We also expect a reference to Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
messages.Senegal: Senegal supports the 30-day technical extension as a necessary bridge to prevent a gap in the Joint Investigative Mechanism's work and to allow the Council to consider improvements in a constructive spirit. We would have preferred a longer renewal, but we believe this text preserves the Mechanism's mandate and the imperative of accountability. We urge all members to unite behind it.
messages.Sweden: Sweden supports this 30-day extension as a necessary bridge and urges all members to vote in favour. We ask that OP2 be adjusted so that the requested report cannot be read as questioning the JIM’s independence or as a precondition for future renewal. With that safeguard, Sweden is ready to support the text.
messages.Ukraine: Ukraine supports the 30-day technical rollover as necessary to avoid any gap in the JIM’s work and to preserve the only Council mechanism identifying perpetrators of chemical weapons use in Syria. We ask that the text explicitly preserve the Mechanism’s operational independence and make clear that the review and future mandate discussion cannot be used to undermine, condition or delay accountability. Our red line is any language that could be exploited to weaken the JIM or shield perpetrators from justice.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports this draft as a necessary technical extension to keep the Joint Investigative Mechanism's work alive and to preserve accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria. We urge all Council members to support it without further conditions or delay. We would have preferred a longer renewal, but we will not seek changes that risk this compromise.
messages.United States of America: The United States supports a clean 30-day technical rollover to keep the JIM alive, but we cannot accept language that echoes Russian criticism of the JIM's impartiality. Please delete the 'ensuring its impartiality, professionalism and objectivity' clause in OP2 and replace it with language confirming that any review is without prejudice to the JIM's independence, mandate and prior findings. We also ask that OP4 be strengthened to 'demands' full cooperation and safe access.
messages.Uruguay: Uruguay supports the draft as a pragmatic step to prevent a gap in the JIM's work and to preserve its capacity to identify perpetrators of chemical weapons use. We urge the Council to adopt it without delay so that the Mechanism's staff and operations can continue. We would have preferred a longer extension, but given the impasse, this 30-day rollover is the responsible course.

steps.summary: Japan revised the draft to preserve the Joint Investigative Mechanism's independence and accountability while incorporating technical methodology, non-politicization and independence safeguards. The text accommodates most requests from China, Egypt, Sweden, Ukraine and the United States, but rejects Russia's demand to suspend attribution and Bolivia's operative conditions. It is expected to receive 13 votes in favour, with Russia and Bolivia opposing.

The Security Council,
Recalling its resolutions 2118 (2013), 2209 (2015), 2235 (2015) and 2319 (2016), and all other relevant resolutions,
Reaffirming the paramount importance of the Charter of the United Nations and the obligation of all Member States to refrain from the threat or use of force,
Reaffirming that the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security,
Recalling the establishment by resolution 2235 (2015) of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism to identify individuals, entities, groups or governments responsible for the use of chemicals as weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic,
Recalling the extension of the mandate of the Joint Investigative Mechanism by resolution 2319 (2016),
Welcoming the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons in establishing facts and identifying perpetrators,
Stressing the need for accountability for all use of chemical weapons,
Noting the Security Council’s discussions on improving the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, including at its meeting on 7 November 2017,
Recognizing the need for the Joint Investigative Mechanism to continue its work in an impartial, professional and objective manner,
Emphasizing that the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism must be conducted in a comprehensive, objective and impartial manner and must not be politicized, and that all parties should cooperate fully with the Mechanism,
Reaffirming its respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of the Syrian Arab Republic,
Determining that the situation in the Syrian Arab Republic continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security,
Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,

1. Decides to extend the mandate of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism, as set out in resolution 2235 (2015) and extended by resolution 2319 (2016), for a technical and temporary period of 30 days, until 16 December 2017, without prejudice to the Council’s consideration of the future mandate of the Mechanism; stresses that this extension is a technical rollover to avoid any interruption in the Mechanism’s work and shall not be used to condition, delay or prejudice the renewal of its mandate;
2. Requests the Secretary-General, in coordination with the Director-General of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, to submit to the Security Council within 15 days a report on ways to improve the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, including its working methods and procedures, in particular field visits to sites of alleged incidents, the excavation, recording and collection of evidence and samples, the study of all possible scenarios related to incidents of the use of chemical weapons, and the use of scientific and rational methods, with a view to ensuring that the Mechanism’s conclusions are comprehensive, reliable, credible and based on solid evidence, without prejudice to the Mechanism’s independence, mandate and prior findings, and without prejudging its findings or the future renewal of its mandate, while fully respecting its impartiality, professionalism and objectivity, and ensuring non-politicization; and to provide recommendations on the future mandate of the Mechanism, which the Council will consider in its deliberations on the future mandate;
3. Reaffirms that the Joint Investigative Mechanism shall continue to identify, to the extent possible, individuals, entities, groups or governments responsible for the use of chemicals as weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, in an impartial, professional and objective manner, and that all perpetrators of the use of chemical weapons must be held accountable;
4. Demands that all parties in the Syrian Arab Republic cooperate fully with the Joint Investigative Mechanism and ensure safe and unhindered access for its personnel;
5. Reaffirms its commitment to the full implementation of resolution 2118 (2013) and all other relevant resolutions;
6. Reaffirms that the Joint Investigative Mechanism must continue to carry out its mandate independently and without political interference, and that any discussion of its working methods shall not be used to undermine its credibility or to shield perpetrators from accountability;
7. Decides to remain actively seized of the matter.

messages.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia supports the 30-day technical rollover and the safeguards against politicization. We ask only to strengthen the existing sovereignty paragraph with explicit reference to national unity and non-interference, which are core principles and do not affect the Mechanism's independence. With that preambular clarification, Bolivia can support the draft.
messages.China: China supports the revised draft as a technical and temporary rollover of the JIM mandate, which helps avoid interruption in the Mechanism’s work. The accepted language on non-politicization, scientific methods, field investigations and solid evidence addresses our key concerns. We urge the JIM to continue its work in an impartial, objective and professional manner and call on all parties to cooperate fully. China will vote in favour.
messages.Egypt: Egypt supports the revised draft as a technical rollover that avoids interrupting the Joint Investigative Mechanism’s work while preserving its independence. We welcome the incorporation in OP2 of field visits, evidence collection and the study of all possible scenarios, which are essential to credible and non-politicized investigations. Egypt calls on all members to support this consensus text and to ensure that the Mechanism can continue its mandate without political interference.
messages.Ethiopia: Ethiopia supports the revised draft as a pragmatic technical rollover that avoids interrupting the Joint Investigative Mechanism’s work while allowing the Council to consider its future mandate. We welcome the text’s reaffirmation of the Mechanism’s independence, impartiality and accountability for chemical weapons use, and we urge all members to preserve Council unity on this issue.
messages.France: France supports the revised text. The 30-day technical rollover is necessary to avoid any interruption in the Joint Investigative Mechanism’s work and is without prejudice to the Council’s consideration of its future mandate. We welcome the safeguards reaffirming the Mechanism’s independence and prior findings, and we call on all members to support the text.
messages.Italy: Italy supports the current text as a pragmatic and balanced technical rollover that preserves the continuity of the Joint Investigative Mechanism and its crucial work on accountability. The safeguards in the text make clear that this extension must not condition, delay or prejudice future renewal, and that the Mechanism’s independence, impartiality and prior findings must be fully respected. We therefore encourage all Council members to support the draft without further changes.
messages.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan supports the revised draft as a balanced technical rollover that avoids an interruption in the JIM’s work while allowing the Council to consider improvements and the future mandate. We welcome the emphasis on impartiality, objectivity, non-politicization and full cooperation, and we have no further changes to request. We urge all members to support the text so that the Council can act with one voice.
messages.Russian Federation: We cannot support the revised text as it stands. The proposed 30-day technical rollover must not become a vehicle for continued attribution; OP3 must be replaced as we proposed. We also require OP1 to exclude any automatic renewal and OP2 to make clear that the Council will consider the report before any decision on a future mandate. Without these changes, Russia will not support the draft.
messages.Senegal: Senegal supports the current text as a balanced compromise that preserves the Joint Investigative Mechanism’s independence, impartiality and accountability role while allowing a technical rollover to avoid any interruption in its work. We welcome the safeguards in OP2 and OP6 that the discussion of working methods must not prejudice prior findings or shield perpetrators. Senegal therefore encourages all Council members to support the draft without further changes.
messages.Sweden: Sweden thanks the penholder for revising OP2 to preserve the Mechanism’s independence and to avoid prejudging its findings or future renewal. Sweden supports the current text as a necessary technical rollover and will vote in favour. We stress that the 30-day extension must not become a pretext to weaken or terminate the JIM; the Council must return promptly to renew its mandate and uphold accountability. We call on all members to cooperate in good faith and not to block this technical extension.
messages.Ukraine: Ukraine supports the revised draft as circulated. The OP1 technical-rollover safeguard and the OP6 language on the Mechanism’s independence and on not shielding perpetrators address our red lines, and the OP2 safeguards on prior findings and non-politicization are important. We urge the Council to adopt the text without further dilution so that the Joint Investigative Mechanism can continue its impartial and objective work.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports the draft as circulated. This technical rollover is necessary to avoid any interruption in the Joint Investigative Mechanism’s work, and its safeguards against conditioning or prejudicing renewal are important. We urge all Council members to support the text and allow the Mechanism to continue its vital work.
messages.United States of America: The United States supports revision 1 as a balanced technical rollover that preserves the Joint Investigative Mechanism’s independence and prior findings while demanding full cooperation from all parties. We appreciate the penholder’s acceptance of our OP2 safeguards and the strengthened OP4 language. The Council should adopt this text without further delay so the Mechanism’s work is not interrupted.
messages.Uruguay: Uruguay supports the revised text. A 30-day technical rollover is the minimum necessary to avoid another interruption in the JIM’s work and to retain its staff, and we welcome the safeguards in OP6 preserving the Mechanism’s independence and prior findings. We have no further changes and call for its adoption without delay.

replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: accommodated OP1/OP2 procedural points, but rejected the OP3 red line because it would suspend JIM attribution and undermine accountability

steps.summary: The revised text accommodates Bolivia and some Russian procedural points while preserving the JIM’s core attribution mandate. Russia is expected to vote against because OP3 was retained, so the draft would likely receive 14 votes in favour and 1 against, with Russia’s negative vote blocking adoption.

reasons.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia historically voted against the Japanese draft extending the JIM for 30 days, aligning with Russia in viewing the mechanism as politicized and insufficiently reformed. This overrides its earlier conditional negotiation stance, which did not hold at the final vote.
reasons.China: China has consistently supported extending the JIM with improved working methods and safeguards against politicization; the Japanese draft reflects these concerns through a short technical rollover and a report on improving procedures.
reasons.Egypt: Egypt supported the Japanese draft in negotiations and it reflects Egypt's key concerns on improving JIM methodology, field visits, non-politicization, and accountability. A technical rollover also prevents a gap while preserving the Council's ability to discuss the future mandate.
reasons.Ethiopia: Ethiopia has consistently supported renewing the JIM and was listed as supporting this draft in the last negotiation round; the draft is a technical rollover consistent with its stated priority of avoiding a gap in accountability. Ethiopia would likely explain its vote to stress support for the Mechanism while criticizing politicization.
reasons.France: France had supported the previous JIM renewal draft and opposed Russian/Bolivian alternatives, and it recorded support for this Japanese draft in negotiations, so it votes yes to prevent an interruption in the Mechanism’s work.
reasons.Italy: Italy has consistently supported the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism and voted for prior renewal efforts; this technical rollover aligns with its position despite objections to a short extension. It would likely explain its vote in favour to urge continued unity and accountability.
reasons.Japan: Japan authored the compromise rollover draft and has consistently prioritized keeping the JIM operational and ensuring accountability for chemical weapons use. As the submitting delegation, Japan would explain its vote and call for unity before the vote.
reasons.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has consistently supported preserving the JIM and voted in favour of the 16 November extension drafts; it was also recorded as supporting this compromise in negotiations. The 30-day technical rollover with a report on improving working methods is consistent with Kazakhstan’s emphasis on accountability, non-politicization and avoiding an interruption in the Mechanism’s work.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia’s red-line request to suspend JIM attribution during the 30-day rollover was rejected, so voting against is consistent with its prior vetoes and stated position. The draft keeps OP3 attribution language that Russia regards as politicized and unacceptable.
reasons.Senegal: Senegal has consistently supported renewing the JIM and voted for prior compromise texts; this draft aligns with its emphasis on accountability, impartiality, and avoiding an interruption in the Mechanism’s work.
reasons.Sweden: Sweden has consistently supported the JIM and accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria, including backing previous extension drafts and opposing alternatives it saw as undermining the Mechanism. This draft is a technical extension that preserves the JIM pending further Council consideration, so Sweden votes yes.
reasons.Ukraine: Ukraine’s vote follows its strong record of supporting the JIM’s mandate and accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria, while insisting that any extension or procedural review not undermine the Mechanism’s independence. The draft is a temporary rollover and was recorded as supported by Ukraine in the last negotiation round.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The UK has consistently supported renewal of the JIM and voted for prior technical rollover drafts; this Japanese draft is compatible with that policy and the UK’s position in the last negotiation round was support.
reasons.United States of America: The United States strongly supported the JIM and had just blamed Russia for obstructing its renewal, so it would back Japan’s technical 30-day rollover to preserve the Mechanism while pressing for accountability. Since the draft matches the U.S. position in the last negotiation round, a pre-vote statement in favour is appropriate.
reasons.Uruguay: Uruguay’s record and last-round position strongly support renewing the JIM, and it voted for similar efforts while opposing a rival draft. A 30-day technical rollover aligns with Uruguay’s stated priority of avoiding interruption and preserving accountability.

steps.text:
The Security Council,
Recalling its resolutions 2118 (2013), 2209 (2015), 2235 (2015) and 2319 (2016), and all other relevant resolutions,
Reaffirming the paramount importance of the Charter of the United Nations and the obligation of all Member States to refrain from the threat or use of force,
Reaffirming that the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security,
Recalling the establishment by resolution 2235 (2015) of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism to identify individuals, entities, groups or governments responsible for the use of chemicals as weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic,
Recalling the extension of the mandate of the Joint Investigative Mechanism by resolution 2319 (2016),
Welcoming the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons in establishing facts and identifying perpetrators,
Stressing the need for accountability for all use of chemical weapons,
Noting the Security Council’s discussions on improving the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, including at its meeting on 7 November 2017,
Recognizing the need for the Joint Investigative Mechanism to continue its work in an impartial, professional and objective manner,
Emphasizing that the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism must be conducted in a comprehensive, objective and impartial manner and must not be politicized, and that all parties should cooperate fully with the Mechanism,
Reaffirming its respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, political independence and national unity of the Syrian Arab Republic and the principle of non-interference in its internal affairs,
Determining that the situation in the Syrian Arab Republic continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security,
Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,

1. Decides to extend the mandate of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism, as set out in resolution 2235 (2015) and extended by resolution 2319 (2016), for a technical and temporary period of 30 days, until 16 December 2017, without prejudice to the Council’s consideration of the future mandate of the Mechanism and without any automatic renewal; stresses that this extension is a technical rollover to avoid any interruption in the Mechanism’s work and shall not be used to condition, delay or prejudice the renewal of its mandate;
2. Requests the Secretary-General, in coordination with the Director-General of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, to submit to the Security Council within 15 days a report on ways to improve the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, including its working methods and procedures, in particular field visits to sites of alleged incidents, the excavation, recording and collection of evidence and samples, the study of all possible scenarios related to incidents of the use of chemical weapons, and the use of scientific and rational methods, with a view to ensuring that the Mechanism’s conclusions are comprehensive, reliable, credible and based on solid evidence, without prejudice to the Mechanism’s independence, mandate and prior findings, and without prejudging its findings or the future renewal of its mandate, while fully respecting its impartiality, professionalism and objectivity, and ensuring non-politicization; and to provide recommendations on the future mandate of the Mechanism; decides that the Council shall consider this report in its deliberations before taking any decision on a future mandate;
3. Reaffirms that the Joint Investigative Mechanism shall continue to identify, to the extent possible, individuals, entities, groups or governments responsible for the use of chemicals as weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, in an impartial, professional and objective manner, and that all perpetrators of the use of chemical weapons must be held accountable;
4. Demands that all parties in the Syrian Arab Republic cooperate fully with the Joint Investigative Mechanism and ensure safe and unhindered access for its personnel;
5. Reaffirms its commitment to the full implementation of resolution 2118 (2013) and all other relevant resolutions;
6. Reaffirms that the Joint Investigative Mechanism must continue to carry out its mandate independently and without political interference, and that any discussion of its working methods shall not be used to undermine its credibility or to shield perpetrators from accountability;
7. Decides to remain actively seized of the matter.

before.China: China will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We firmly oppose the use of chemical weapons by any party, under any circumstances. The Joint Investigative Mechanism should continue its work in an objective, impartial and professional manner. We support a technical rollover to avoid interruption of the Mechanism’s work, and we believe the requested report on improving working methods, including evidence collection and field visits, is constructive. At the same time, the work of the Mechanism must not be politicized, its independence must be respected, and its conclusions must be based on solid evidence and stand the test of time. China supports accountability for all chemical weapons attacks in Syria and calls on all parties to cooperate fully with the Mechanism.
before.Egypt: Egypt will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We support a technical and temporary extension of the Joint Investigative Mechanism so that its work is not interrupted and so that the Council can consider, in a calm and objective manner, ways to improve its working methods. Egypt has consistently stressed that the Mechanism must act with impartiality, professionalism and objectivity, without politicization, and that its investigations must be comprehensive and based on solid evidence, including field visits, the collection of samples and the study of all possible scenarios. We also reaffirm that all perpetrators of the use of chemical weapons must be held accountable, while the sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence of the Syrian Arab Republic must be respected. We call on all parties to cooperate fully with the Mechanism and urge the Council to use the coming period to reach consensus on the future of its mandate.
before.Ethiopia: Ethiopia will vote in favour of the draft resolution. We support the extension of the Joint Investigative Mechanism because credible allegations of the use of chemical weapons in Syria remain unresolved, and accountability must not be allowed to lapse. We regard this 30-day technical rollover as a necessary step to avoid any interruption in the Mechanism’s work while the Council considers improvements to its working methods and its future mandate. At the same time, we stress that the Mechanism must remain impartial, professional and objective, and that discussions on working methods must not be used to undermine its credibility or to shield perpetrators from accountability. We call on all parties to cooperate fully with the Mechanism and urge the Council to overcome politicization and preserve its unity in addressing this serious threat.
before.France: France will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The use of chemical weapons is a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security, and those responsible must be held accountable. The Joint Investigative Mechanism must be able to continue its essential work without interruption. France therefore supports this 30-day technical extension, which is necessary to avoid a gap in the Mechanism’s work while the Council considers ways to strengthen its working methods and the future of its mandate. We reiterate that the Mechanism must continue to act in an impartial, professional and objective manner, and that no discussion of its methods should be used to undermine its credibility or to shield perpetrators from accountability.
before.Italy: Italy will vote in favour of the draft resolution before us. The Joint Investigative Mechanism must be able to continue its essential work without interruption, and we support this technical extension as a means to preserve the Mechanism’s capacity and expertise while the Council considers its future mandate. Italy remains firmly committed to accountability for all use of chemical weapons and stresses that the Mechanism must continue to act impartially, professionally and objectively, without politicization and without interference. We regret that the Council has not yet been able to agree on a full and predictable renewal, and we call on all members to work in good faith to ensure that the Mechanism can continue to fulfil its mandate.
before.Japan: Japan will vote in favour of this draft resolution, which we have submitted as a technical and temporary 30-day rollover to prevent any interruption in the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism. This text does not prejudge the future mandate of the Mechanism; rather, it provides the Council with a short window to consider improvements to its working methods while preserving the Mechanism’s independence, impartiality and professionalism. Japan has listened carefully to the concerns expressed by Council members and has sought a balanced text that upholds accountability for all use of chemical weapons. We stress that the Mechanism’s findings must not be politicized and that all parties in Syria must cooperate fully with it. We urge all members to support this draft so that the Council does not allow impunity for the use of chemical weapons.
before.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan supports the draft resolution before the Council. We have consistently supported the continuation of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism, as accountability for the use of chemical weapons is essential and there is no alternative to objective, impartial and professional investigation. This technical rollover is necessary to avoid an interruption in the Mechanism’s work, and we welcome the request for a report on improving its working methods, including field visits, evidence-gathering and scientific rigour. It is important that these discussions strengthen the credibility of the Mechanism and are not used to politicize or prejudge its findings or future mandate. We call on all parties to cooperate fully and urge the Council to preserve its unity in addressing chemical weapons in Syria.
before.Russian Federation: Mr. President, the Russian Federation cannot support this draft. It does not address the fundamental concerns we have repeatedly raised regarding the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, and it ignores the minimum requirement that a technical rollover must not be used to cement attribution while the Council considers genuine reform. We remain in favour of an impartial, professional and non-politicized mechanism, but the draft before us retains provisions that prejudge the outcome and undermine the effort to restore confidence in the Mechanism. We will therefore vote against.
before.Senegal: Senegal wishes to thank Japan for its efforts to bridge the differences within the Council. We support this draft resolution because the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism must be able to continue its impartial, independent and objective work without interruption. The continued allegations of chemical weapons use in Syria and the suffering of the Syrian people require the Council to avoid any vacuum in accountability. A technical and temporary 30-day extension does not prejudge the future mandate of the Mechanism, but it preserves the possibility of a unified decision and ensures that the Mechanism’s work is not halted while the Council examines ways to improve its methods. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully with the Mechanism and on all Council members to uphold accountability. Senegal will vote in favour of this draft resolution.
before.Sweden: Sweden will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The Joint Investigative Mechanism must be able to continue its vital work without interruption. This technical and temporary extension is necessary to preserve the Mechanism’s ability to establish facts and identify perpetrators, and to allow the Council time to consider improvements to its working methods without undermining its independence, impartiality or prior findings. Sweden remains firmly committed to accountability for all use of chemical weapons in Syria. We regret that the Council has been unable to unite earlier, but we support this effort to avoid a gap in the Mechanism’s mandate.
before.Ukraine: Ukraine votes in favour of this draft resolution. We have consistently supported the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism as an indispensable accountability tool in the Syrian Arab Republic. A technical 30-day rollover should prevent an interruption in the Mechanism’s work, and it must not be used to undermine its independence, objectivity or prior findings. We stress that any discussion of improving the Mechanism’s working methods must strengthen, not politicize or micromanage, its work. All parties must cooperate fully, and all perpetrators of chemical weapons use must be held accountable.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom votes in favour of this draft resolution. The Joint Investigative Mechanism has a clear and vital mandate: to identify those responsible for the use of chemical weapons in Syria so that they can be held accountable. A 30-day technical rollover is not a substitute for a full renewal, but it avoids an unnecessary interruption in the Mechanism’s work and preserves the space for the Council to consider how best to take that work forward. We support the text submitted by Japan, which safeguards the JIM’s independence and prior findings while allowing a serious discussion of its working methods. We urge all members of this Council to support it.
before.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism is essential to accountability for the use of chemical weapons in Syria, and a 30-day technical extension will prevent an interruption in its work while the Council considers the way forward. We thank Japan for its efforts to bridge differences. The United States stresses that this extension is not a substitute for a full and independent mandate. The Mechanism must continue to identify perpetrators in an impartial, professional and objective manner; its prior findings must not be reopened, conditioned or politicized, and its working methods must not be used to shield anyone from accountability. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully and ensure safe and unhindered access. The United States remains committed to ensuring that those who use chemical weapons are held accountable.
before.Uruguay: Uruguay will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We have consistently supported the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons-United Nations Joint Investigative Mechanism, and we believe that a technical rollover is the minimum necessary to avoid interrupting its vital work and to protect the staff who carry it out. The Mechanism’s independence, impartiality, professionalism and objectivity must be preserved. Uruguay regrets that the Council has again been forced to confront this situation at the last minute, and we urge all parties to cooperate fully with the Mechanism. Accountability for the use of chemical weapons cannot be delayed or made conditional. We support this extension so that the Council may consider the future mandate seriously, without politicization and without undermining the Mechanism’s credibility or prior findings.

after.Bolivia (Plurinational State of):
Mr. President,

Bolivia (Plurinational State of) voted against this draft resolution and wishes to explain its position.

The use of chemical weapons is a grave violation of international law and must never remain unpunished. Bolivia reaffirms its categorical rejection of the use of chemical weapons by any actor, under any circumstances. But accountability cannot be built on politicization, selectivity or double standards. The work of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism must be impartial, objective, professional and based on solid and verifiable evidence; it must fully respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of the Syrian Arab Republic and the principle of non-interference in its internal affairs.

We did not support this text because it did not adequately address the serious concerns that have been raised about the working methods, credibility and politicization of the Mechanism, and because a so-called technical rollover cannot be transformed into a means of conditioning the Council’s future decision or of legitimizing politically motivated accusations before a serious, transparent and balanced discussion of the Mechanism’s mandate and methods has taken place.

Bolivia regrets that the Council could not reach consensus. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully with the relevant international bodies, and we reaffirm that there can be no impunity while the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Syria are fully respected. Bolivia will continue to oppose the politicization of chemical weapons issues and any attempt to use them as a pretext for intervention or regime change.
after.China: Thank you, Mr. President. China voted in favour of the draft resolution submitted by Japan. We regret that the draft was not adopted, as this has interrupted the mandated work of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism at a critical time. China firmly opposes the use of chemical weapons by any country, organization or individual under any circumstances, and supports accountability for all chemical-weapons attacks in Syria. The Mechanism should continue to carry out its work in a comprehensive, objective, impartial and professional manner, with conclusions based on solid evidence that can withstand the test of time and reality. A technical rollover would have avoided a gap in the Mechanism’s work while the Council considered how to improve its working methods, including field visits, evidence collection and scientific rigour. At the same time, the Mechanism’s work must not be politicized, and the concerns raised by Council members should be properly addressed. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully with the Mechanism and on all Council members to maintain unity, engage in full consultations and find a proper solution on the future mandate of the Mechanism as soon as possible.
after.France:
Mr. President,

France deeply regrets that this draft resolution was not adopted solely because of the veto of the Russian Federation. Thirteen members of this Council supported a technical and temporary 30-day rollover: a balanced text that did not prejudge the future mandate of the Joint Investigative Mechanism and that safeguarded its independence and prior findings. It was the minimum necessary to prevent an interruption in the Mechanism’s essential work.

The Russian veto creates a gap in accountability. It is particularly serious because it comes as the Council is still discussing how to improve the Mechanism’s working methods. Those discussions must never become a pretext for undermining the Mechanism or shielding perpetrators. The use of chemical weapons in Syria is a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security. France will not accept impunity.

We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully with the Mechanism and on all members of this Council to resume work without delay on a full and independent renewal of its mandate. The credibility of this Council is at stake.
after.Italy: Mr. President, Italy regrets that the Security Council has not been able to adopt the draft resolution before us. We voted in favour because the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism must be able to continue its essential work without interruption. This technical and temporary extension was intended to preserve the Mechanism’s capacity and expertise while the Council considers its future mandate. The use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security, and those responsible must be held accountable. Italy remains firmly committed to the Mechanism and stresses that it must continue to act impartially, professionally and objectively, without politicization or political interference. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully with the Mechanism and on all Council members to overcome divisions and to work in good faith to ensure that the Mechanism can continue to fulfil its mandate.
after.Japan:
Mr. President,

Japan takes the floor as the penholder of the draft resolution just put to the vote. We deeply regret that the Security Council has again failed to overcome its divisions and that this draft resolution was not adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent member. Thirteen members voted in favour of a technical and temporary 30-day rollover whose purpose was precisely to prevent any interruption in the work of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism and to preserve the Council’s space to consider improvements to its working methods, without prejudging the Mechanism’s future mandate or its prior findings.

This was a reasonable and necessary step. Its rejection means that the Mechanism cannot continue its essential work at a time when allegations of chemical weapons use in Syria remain unresolved. Japan’s position is unchanged: the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security, and it cannot go unpunished. The Mechanism must be able to carry out its mandate impartially, professionally and objectively, and all parties in Syria must cooperate fully with it.

There is no changing the fact that the Council remains ultimately responsible for ensuring accountability for the use of chemical weapons. Japan urges all members not to abandon our efforts to prevent the further use of chemical weapons and not to allow impunity. We will continue to work with all members to find a way forward.
after.Kazakhstan: Mr. President, Kazakhstan voted in favour of the draft resolution submitted by Japan. We did so because we firmly believe that the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism must be able to continue its work without interruption and that accountability for the use of chemical weapons cannot be allowed to lapse. A 30-day technical rollover was a modest, practical and balanced step. It did not prejudge the future mandate of the Mechanism, nor did it seek to politicize its work. It was intended to preserve the Mechanism’s expertise and give the Council time to consider improvements to its working methods in a calm and objective manner. We regret that the draft was not adopted. The result again demonstrates the deep divisions within the Council on this important issue. Kazakhstan respects the positions of all members, but we cannot hide our concern that the Mechanism’s work may now be interrupted. We call on all parties to continue consultations in good faith, to avoid creating a vacuum in accountability, and to work towards a unified decision that preserves the independence, impartiality, professionalism and credibility of the Mechanism. The fight against chemical weapons must remain above politics, and the Council must not fail those who expect us to act with a single voice.
after.Russian Federation:
Mr. President,

The Russian Federation has voted against the draft resolution just put to the vote, and I wish to explain our position. We fully share the goal of preventing the use of chemical weapons and ensuring accountability for any such use in Syria. Russia has consistently supported the destruction of Syria’s chemical weapons programme and the work of the OPCW. But we cannot support a text that, while described as a technical rollover, in fact seeks to preserve the Joint Investigative Mechanism in its current flawed form and to predetermine the outcome of any future discussion of its mandate.

The draft did not address the fundamental concerns that we have raised repeatedly. It did not provide for a genuine review of the Mechanism’s working methods; it sought instead to shield its prior findings from scrutiny and to make discussion of its shortcomings conditional. The JIM has suffered from a lack of transparency, insufficient work on the ground, reliance on questionable sources and persistent politicization. Russia’s proposals were intended to make the Mechanism professional, impartial and credible. Our alternative draft S/2017/933 was before the Council from 7 November, but our partners preferred to rush to a vote and to continue a campaign of accusations against Russia.

We reject the attempts to blame the Russian Federation for the fact that the mandate has lapsed. The mandate has lapsed because some delegations insisted on maintaining a mechanism that has discredited itself and on turning the Security Council into an instrument of political pressure. Russia is ready to work on a new mandate based on the OPCW Convention, respect for Syria’s sovereignty and reliable, verifiable evidence. But we will not support a text that institutionalizes bias and prejudges the outcome.

Thank you.
after.Senegal: Senegal regrets that the Security Council has once again been unable to preserve its unity on the mandate of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism. We voted in favour of the draft resolution submitted by Japan because the Mechanism must be able to continue its independent, impartial and objective work without interruption. The proposed 30-day extension was technical and temporary; it did not prejudge the future mandate of the Mechanism. It was a minimum step to avoid a vacuum in accountability while the Council considered ways to improve the Mechanism’s working methods. The continued allegations of chemical weapons use in Syria and the suffering of the Syrian people make it imperative that the Mechanism’s work not be halted. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully with the Mechanism, and on all Council members to return to the spirit of consensus so that accountability for the use of chemical weapons is neither weakened nor politicized.
after.Sweden: Mr. President, Sweden voted in favour of the draft resolution before the Council. We deeply regret that it has not been adopted. This was a technical and temporary 30-day rollover, designed to prevent an interruption in the work of the Joint Investigative Mechanism while the Council considered its future mandate and ways to improve its working methods. It did not prejudge those discussions, and it preserved the Mechanism’s independence, impartiality and prior findings. The Council’s inability to adopt even this modest text is a serious setback for accountability and for the credibility of this Council. The use of chemical weapons is a grave violation of international law. There must be no impunity for those responsible. The victims of chemical weapons attacks in Syria deserve accountability, and the credibility of the international disarmament architecture requires it. Sweden will continue to support the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism and its essential work. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully, and we urge all Council members not to let the Mechanism lapse. We must return to this matter immediately and in good faith. The Council must speak with one voice against chemical weapons. Thank you.
after.Ukraine:
Mr. President,

Ukraine voted in favour of the draft resolution submitted by Japan because the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism must be allowed to continue its indispensable work without interruption. We deeply regret that the Council has once again been prevented from taking even this technical and temporary step, owing to the negative vote of the Russian Federation.

This veto does not serve the cause of impartiality or reform; it creates a dangerous gap in accountability and sends a signal to those who use chemical weapons that the Council can be paralysed and that perpetrators may escape justice. Ukraine has consistently supported the Joint Investigative Mechanism as the only international tool mandated to identify the perpetrators of chemical weapons use in Syria. Any discussion of improving its working methods must strengthen, not politicize, micromanage or undermine the Mechanism’s independence, objectivity, credibility or prior findings.

We call on all parties in the Syrian Arab Republic to cooperate fully with the Mechanism and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, and we reaffirm that all perpetrators of chemical weapons use must be held accountable. The Security Council must not allow accountability to become a hostage to political protection.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
Thank you, Mr President. The United Kingdom voted in favour of this draft, and we deeply regret that it has not been adopted. This was a modest, technical and temporary 30-day rollover. It did not prejudge the future mandate of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, nor did it seek to condition its findings. It was designed to do exactly what the Council should have been able to agree: prevent an interruption in the work of an impartial mechanism while we discussed its working methods and future mandate.

Russia’s veto has blocked that modest step. It has ensured that the JIM cannot continue its work. That is a veto against accountability and against the principle that chemical weapons must never be used with impunity. We thank Japan for its efforts to bridge the Council’s differences, and we regret that those efforts have been rejected.

The United Kingdom will not abandon the search for accountability. We will continue to support the OPCW and all credible efforts to identify and hold accountable those responsible for chemical weapons attacks in Syria. The victims of these attacks, including in Khan Shaykhun, deserve no less. Thank you.
after.United States of America:
Mr. President,

The United States voted in favour of this resolution, and we deeply regret that it was not adopted. Thirteen members of this Council supported a technical, time-limited extension to prevent a gap in the work of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism. Russia has once again used its veto — not to defend the integrity of the Mechanism, but to ensure that its work cannot continue. In doing so, Russia has killed the JIM.

Let us be clear: this was a reasonable and limited text. It did not prejudge the JIM’s future mandate. It did not reopen the JIM’s prior findings. It simply preserved the Mechanism’s ability to continue its work for 30 days while the Council considered improvements to its working methods. There was no legitimate justification for a veto.

Russia’s veto does not erase the facts. The JIM has already established that chemical weapons have been used in Syria and has identified perpetrators. Those findings stand. They are not reversed by a veto. Russia cannot veto the truth, and it cannot veto the obligation under resolution 2118 to hold accountable those who use chemical weapons.

The United States will continue to support the OPCW, the JIM’s essential work, and all credible efforts to ensure accountability. We will not accept impunity for the use of chemical weapons. We call on Russia to stop shielding the Assad regime and to work with this Council in good faith. The victims of chemical weapons deserve better than a veto, and this Council should not allow the Joint Investigative Mechanism to become another casualty of Russian obstruction.

Thank you.
after.Uruguay: Uruguay regrets that the Security Council has once again been unable to preserve the mandate of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism, even through a technical and temporary rollover. We voted in favour of the draft submitted by Japan because it was a pragmatic and minimal step: it would have prevented an interruption in the Mechanism’s work, protected its staff and preserved the Council’s ability to consider its future mandate seriously. The use of chemical weapons is a serious violation of international law, and accountability cannot be made conditional or delayed. Uruguay reiterates its full confidence in the impartiality, professionalism and objectivity of the Mechanism and its prior findings. We call on all parties in Syria to cooperate fully, and we reaffirm our view that the veto should not be used in cases of mass atrocity. The Council must not allow impunity to prevail.
